meta.location: The land of Nephi, under Lamanite tribute

world_behind.title: A prophecy fulfilled line by line
world_behind.text: Abinadi had said this generation would be brought into bondage, smitten on the cheek, driven by men, with burdens lashed on their backs, driven like a dumb ass. Verse 3 lists the same items in nearly the same words, and verse 4 states outright that all this was done so the word of the Lord might be fulfilled. The abridger does more than draw a parallel. He declares the prophecy settled.

world_behind.title: What the oath actually bought
world_behind.text: The Lamanite king had sworn not to slay Limhi's people. Verse 3 says they durst not kill them because of that oath, and then lists everything they did instead. An oath against killing turns out to be compatible with forced labor, beatings, and armed encirclement.

world_behind.title: Three defeats and a demographic collapse
world_behind.text: The people press the king into war three separate times and lose each one. By verse 17 there are more women than men in the land. The bondage described in the rest of the chapter is partly self-inflicted, and the record says so without editorializing.

world_behind.title: Relief for widows, by decree
world_behind.text: Limhi orders a standing obligation from every man toward the households the wars emptied. It is the same practice Alma established at the waters of Mormon, arriving here as royal policy in a subject state rather than as a covenant among volunteers.

world_behind.title: A search party that failed and found something else
world_behind.text: Forty-three men went looking for Zarahemla, missed it, crossed a country covered with bones and ruins, and came back with twenty-four engraved plates. That failure is where the Book of Ether enters this record.

world_behind.title: Two documents being stitched together
world_behind.text: Chapters 7 and 8 gave Ammon's arrival as it happened in Ammon's presence. This chapter is working from the record of Zeniff's colony, which is why the same days come round again carrying different details, including that Limhi nearly had his rescuer executed. The abridger is joining two sources and never stops to say so.

words.text: Dared. The Lamanites durst not slay them, and the restraint is attributed to an oath rather than to mercy. The same verb described Noah's priests two chapters ago, where what stopped them was shame. Both times the word marks a limit somebody sets on himself.

To complain in a low, continuous way, and in this record it is nearly always a prelude to a bad decision. The people murmur, the king is afflicted with their complaints, and he grants them the war they want. The verse says he granted it according to their desires.

Formal, voiced grief, the public counterpart of private mourning. The verse lists who is mourning for whom: widow for husband, son and daughter for father, brothers for brethren. The list is the casualty report.

By stages, a little at a time. They began to prosper by degrees, and the phrase occurs once in scripture. Everything good in this chapter arrives incrementally: eased burdens, more grain, no hunger. Nothing arrives all at once.

To give a share of what you have. Limhi commands every man to impart to the support of the widows and their children. It is the verb Alma used for the same practice three chapters earlier, here issued as a command by a king. Alma's people took it up as a covenant.

Effort and application, not reading. The whole study of Ammon, Limhi, and their people was to deliver themselves out of bondage. The word closes the chapter on a people whose entire attention has one object.

phrases.term: Smite them on their cheeks, and exercise authority over them
phrases.text: Abinadi's sentence arriving in the vocabulary he used. He had said they would be smitten on the cheek and driven like a dumb ass; this verse says both, adds heavy burdens on their backs, and the next verse names it as fulfilment. The clause appears once in scripture.

phrases.term: All this was done that the word of the Lord might be fulfilled
phrases.text: The abridger stepping in to close an account. It is one sentence, it interrupts nothing, and it converts a paragraph of political misery into the settlement of a prophecy delivered nine chapters earlier.

phrases.term: The widow mourning for her husband
phrases.text: The casualty list given as relationships. Four categories, each naming who is left and who is gone. The phrase occurs once in scripture, and the verse that follows says there were a great many widows.

phrases.term: Their continual cries did stir up the remainder of the people
phrases.text: The grief of the bereaved producing more bereavement. The widows' cries move the survivors to fight again, and they lose again. The record lets the causal chain stand without saying anything about it.

phrases.term: The Lord was slow to hear their cry because of their iniquities
phrases.text: Abinadi had said this in advance, in almost these words. The verse then does something unusual: it says the Lord did hear, did soften the Lamanites, did ease the burdens, and did not deliver them. Three partial answers and one refusal, in a single verse.

phrases.term: Yet the Lord did not see fit to deliver them out of bondage
phrases.text: A refusal stated without explanation, and the clause occurs once in scripture. Three chapters later another group in bondage will have their burdens made light so they cannot feel them and will be delivered the next morning. The record puts the two accounts near each other and never compares them.

phrases.term: A land which was covered with dry bones
phrases.text: What the search party found instead of Zarahemla. Ezekiel is shown a valley of dry bones and told to prophesy over them; these men see the same landscape and bring home a record. The chapter treats the discovery as a footnote to a failure.

phrases.term: There was none in the land that had authority from God
phrases.text: The reason a willing king is not baptized. Ammon, who has been in the land a matter of days, declines and calls himself an unworthy servant. The refusal is on grounds of fitness rather than of office. The people covenant anyway, wait, and the ordinance is deferred by four chapters.

verses.label: v. 1–5
verses.title: The prophecy, itemized
verses.text: Peace, then pressure, then a list of specific humiliations that match a sermon delivered nine chapters earlier almost word for word. Verse 4 states the connection outright. Verse 5 gives the military reality: surrounded on every side, with no way out.

verses.label: v. 6–12
verses.title: Three wars, all lost
verses.text: The people murmur the king into battle, are beaten, mourn, are stirred by the mourning into a second battle, lose, and go a third time. The record numbers the attempts and reports the same outcome three times. The repetition says the lesson took a while.

verses.label: v. 13–15
verses.title: Humility, and a partial answer
verses.text: They humble themselves to the dust, submit to the yoke, and cry all day long. What comes back is softened Lamanite hearts and lighter burdens, and an explicit statement that deliverance was withheld. The verse gives the reason for the delay and none for the refusal.

verses.label: v. 16–19
verses.title: Life inside the arrangement
verses.text: Grain, flocks, herds, no hunger, and a rule that every man support the widows. Then the detail that fixes the tone: the king will not go outside his own walls without guards. Prosperity by degrees, inside a cage.

verses.label: v. 20–22
verses.title: Hunting the priests
verses.text: Limhi's people watch the land for the men whose crime brought this on them, and the priests are still raiding, coming in by night for grain and precious things. The grievance has a practical edge as well as a moral one.

verses.label: v. 25–28
verses.title: Bones, plates, and a reader
verses.text: Sent for Zarahemla, lost, came back with a record engraved on plates of ore from a country covered with bones. Limhi's joy at verse 28 is about learning that somebody can read the plates.

verses.label: v. 33–36
verses.title: Willing, and waiting
verses.text: A king and many of his people want baptism and there is nobody to perform it. Ammon refuses on grounds of unworthiness. They covenant anyway, defer the ordinance, and turn their whole attention to getting out.

chapter.title: A prophecy is closed out inside four verses
chapter.text: Bondage, smitten cheeks, burdens on backs, driven like a dumb ass: Abinadi's terms, reused. Then verse 4 names it as fulfilment outright. The record rarely audits its own predictions this openly, and it does it twice in three chapters.

chapter.title: The chapter's most important sentence is a refusal
chapter.text: The Lord heard, softened hearts, and eased burdens, and did not deliver them. Nothing explains the last clause. Three chapters later a different group in the same condition is delivered outright, and the record sets the two accounts side by side without a word of comparison.

chapter.title: Grief produces the next round of grief
chapter.text: The widows' cries stir the survivors into a second defeat, which produces more widows. The record states the sequence plainly and draws nothing from it.

chapter.title: The change of posture comes last
chapter.text: Every attempt to fight out fails; humbling themselves to the dust is what precedes any improvement at all. The improvement is smaller than what they asked for and it is the only thing that comes.

chapter.title: The best thing in the chapter comes out of a failure
chapter.text: A party sent to find Zarahemla misses it entirely and returns with twenty-four plates from a ruined country. That accident is the source of the Book of Ether, and this chapter treats it in three verses.

chapter.title: Two accounts of authority, three chapters apart, neither explained
chapter.text: Alma baptized having authority from the Almighty God. Ammon declines because there is none in the land that has it and he considers himself unworthy. The record asserts both and argues for neither.

chapter.title: The narrative doubles back
chapter.text: Verses 22 through 36 retell Ammon's arrival, already given from the Zarahemla side in chapters 7 and 8, including the detail that Limhi nearly executed him as one of Noah's priests. The overlap is unmarked.

chapter.title: Role in the unit
chapter.text: Chapter 19 put Limhi on a leased throne, 20 was its first crisis, this is the long middle where nothing works, and 22 is Gideon's escape plan. It also stands as the control case for chapters 23 and 24: two peoples in bondage, praying, with different outcomes.

applications.title: Notice when the answer is partial
applications.text: Softened hearts, lighter burdens, no deliverance. If you are waiting for a situation to end, check whether something in it has already been made survivable, and whether you have counted that as an answer.

applications.title: Grief can recruit you into the next mistake
applications.text: The widows' cries produced another battle and more widows. Strong feeling about a real loss is not the same thing as good judgment about what to do next.

applications.title: Three tries is data
applications.text: They fought their way out three times and lost three times before changing approach. If the same method has failed repeatedly, look at the method before adding effort.

applications.title: Improvement by degrees still counts
applications.text: Grain, flocks, no hunger. None of it deliverance, all of it real. Small compounding gains inside a bad situation are worth naming.

applications.title: Fund the people the losses fell on
applications.text: More women than men, so every man contributes to the widows. When a shared failure leaves some people carrying more of it, the response the chapter records is an obligation that stays in force.

applications.title: A failed search can be the useful trip
applications.text: They never found Zarahemla and came back with the record of a lost civilization. Keep track of what you found while looking for something else.

applications.title: Say no on grounds of unworthiness if that is the reason
applications.text: Ammon declined to baptize a willing king. The people covenanted anyway and waited. Declining something you are not positioned to do can leave the good outcome intact.

questions.text: What am I tolerating because the person doing it stopped short of the one thing they promised not to do?
When have I pressed someone into a decision by wearing them down?
What have I done out of grief that made things worse?
Which of my prayers has been answered in a way I did not count?
Where do I not go without guards, and what does that tell me?
What am I waiting on that I could covenant to now?
